name: British Heart Foundation: research, implementation pilots and policy (charityevals, 2025-26)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: research valued as a share of the world's cardiovascular burden (93% of the result at the defaults, spread by world population), UK tobacco policy and NHS implementation pilots (7%).
summary: The British Heart Foundation is the UK's largest charitable funder of heart and circulatory research; this model covers its research grants (£96.2m in the year to March 2026), its Healthcare Implementation Fund pilots in the NHS and its policy work, chiefly its long campaign for the UK's smokefree-generation law. Research is valued as a share of the global cardiovascular burden that a year of the field's research averts sooner, credited by BHF's share of the world's cardiovascular research funding (about 1%); the pilots as the UK burden their successes avert sooner; policy as BHF's share of the health gain of the Tobacco and Vapes Act; the deaths inside every branch's DALYs are valued by age, so mostly old deaths count less than GBD's years lost. The result, about 0.025 years of healthy life per $1,000, is far below the site's global-health median because research results arrive after about 17 years, are shared with the whole field, and are counted as a past average at the next dollar's share; all three branches are discounted for missing data, since none has measured outcomes for BHF's own spending. It is dominated by judgment (how much of the burden a year of research averts, how many years sooner, BHF's share of the field), so the range is wide and the result is mostly uncertainty; its information, support and CPR work is the separate health-and-support model.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: BHF's research spending and its shares of health spending on policy work and implementation pilots in the year to 31 March 2026, with the cost of raising the money (fundraising and the shops' net loss) spread over all its charitable spending. From the audited accounts.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The burden the work addresses: the world's cardiovascular disease for research, since a drug, device or guideline found in the UK is used worldwide; the UK's for the NHS pilots.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: Research: the share of the burden a year of the field's research averts once adopted, how many years sooner it comes, after the wait from funding to practice. Implementation pilots: the share of the UK burden a year's pilots avert once their successes spread, how many years sooner. Policy: the smokefree-generation law, the health its cohorts gain and the share of the campaign that fell in this year.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch has its own trust in the evidence, share of credit and missing-data step (Convention 4): BHF's share of the world's cardiovascular research funding for research, of the resources behind a pilot's adoption for the pilots, of everyone's resources behind the law for policy. The canonical rows are their DALY-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Years of healthy life averted by the year's research, pilots and policy work, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only. The research result is a past average (what a year's grants buy, by what past research achieved), so the next dollar is valued at the shared share of it.

rows.label: Research expenditure, year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: Net research awards (£91.9m: £103.3m of new grants less the expected underspend and discounting of long grants) plus BHF's own research staff and support costs (£4.3m), as the accounts report them for the year (note 4, p. 125). The year's grants fund 247 awards across fellowships, programme, project and clinical grants and BHF's research centres (p. 67).

rows.label: Health expenditure (information, support, CPR, policy), year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: BHF's second charitable activity: awareness, the Heart Matters magazine, the nurse-led Heart Helpline, health information, CPR (RevivR) and the defibrillator network (The Circuit), healthcare implementation grants, and policy and influencing in the four UK nations (p. 67, p. 28-36). Only its policy share is in this model; the rest is british-heart-foundation-charityevals-health.

rows.label: Share of health expenditure that is policy and influencing work
rows.explainer: The accounts don't split health spending by activity. Policy and public affairs teams in four nations (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland), campaigns and BHF's grants to Action on Smoking and Health are a small part of a £54m budget dominated by information, the magazine, the helpline, CPR and implementation grants (£7.8m of health awards, note 11). Our judgment, anchored on a team of a few dozen people at UK charity pay (staff and support costs in health are £12.5m in all, note 4), with grants to ASH on top. The same judgment is in british-heart-foundation-charityevals-health and sets the programme weights in charities/british-heart-foundation.json: change all three together.

rows.label: Share of health spending on Healthcare Implementation Fund pilots
rows.explainer: The fund pays NHS teams to test new ways of delivering care (cholesterol injections in pharmacies, home blood-pressure checks after pregnancy, health checks for taxi drivers, lung screening; p. 22, 29). The accounts give £7.9m of health grants: £1.0m to ASH and £6.9m of other health grants not itemised (note 11), up from £3.0m of health awards the year before (note 4). The fund has awarded £5.74m in all (BHF's fund page, retrieved 2026-11-04), its earliest listed round in March 2024, so roughly £2–3m a year; the rest of the other health grants is most likely community CPR and defibrillator grants (in cpr_share_of_health) and nurse and professional awards. Our judgment: 5% of health spending (£2.7m with its staff), 3% to 13% (the high end if most of the other health grants were pilots). The same judgment as in british-heart-foundation-charityevals-health, which takes this spending out of its cost; keep the two models and the charity record's weights in step.

rows.label: Spending on research, implementation pilots and policy, year to 31 March 2026 (US$)
rows.explainer: Research plus the policy and Healthcare Implementation Fund shares of health spending, in dollars at the 2025 yearly average rate (the year runs April 2025 to March 2026).

rows.label: Net loss of the shops, year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, statement of financial activities summary
source.quote: Retail net (loss)/profit comprises retail net loss of £(6.7)m (2025: £0.0m) and income from donations received in BHF shops of £3.4m (2025: £3.6m)

rows.explainer: BHF runs the UK's largest charity retailer (651 shops). The shops count by their net contribution, not their gross trading (£240.1m of retail costs against similar sales): this year they lost £6.7m on trading (sales less costs), a cost the charity's other income covered, so it is spread over the charitable work like fundraising. Cash donated in the shops (£3.4m) is a donation, not trading, so it isn't netted against the loss. BHF announced in June 2026 the proposed closure of about 150 shops.

Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)

rows.label: Cost of research and policy, including overhead
World burden of cardiovascular disease, DALYs per year (GBD 2023)

source.title: IHME, Global Burden of Disease 2023 (DALYs by cause), via Our World in Data
source.note: World, 2023: 436,235,460 DALYs from cardiovascular diseases (OWID indicator 1156614).
source.cell: World, 2023, indicator 1156614 (Total number of DALYs from cardiovascular diseases)

rows.explainer: Heart and circulatory disease worldwide (ischaemic heart disease, stroke, heart failure and the rest), GBD 2023: 436 million DALYs (GBD 2021: more than 400 million, Lindstrom et al., JACC 2022), the range for GBD's uncertainty. The whole world, because BHF's results (drugs, devices, guidelines) are used wherever such advances reach; uptake outside rich countries is lower, and that is in the share averted, not here.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: UK burden of cardiovascular disease, DALYs per year

source.title: IHME, Global Burden of Disease 2023 (DALYs by cause), via Our World in Data
source.note: United Kingdom, 2023: 3,351,528 DALYs from cardiovascular diseases (OWID indicator 1156614).
source.cell: United Kingdom, 2023, indicator 1156614 (Total number of DALYs from cardiovascular diseases)

rows.explainer: The pilots test care in the NHS, so their reach is the UK's burden: 3.35 million DALYs from heart and circulatory disease in 2023 (GBD 2023), about ±10% for GBD's uncertainty. (BHF's compendium gives the age-standardised rate, 2,138.6 per 100,000 in 2021, lower because the UK is older than the standard population.)

rows.label: Implementation pilots: average cost of a pilot, with the fund's running costs (£)
rows.explainer: The year's named awards are £78,000 (taxi drivers' health checks), £188,000 (lung screening), £195,000 (blood pressure after pregnancy) and £198,000 (cholesterol injections in pharmacies) (p. 22, 29); awards go up to £500,000 and the fund has staff. Our judgment: £200,000 a pilot, £150,000 to £350,000.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: pilots funded in the year
rows.explainer: The fund's spending over the cost of a pilot, so the pilots move with the spending judged.

rows.label: Share of the burden the advances from one year of the field's research avert each year once in use
rows.explainer: One judgment, the product of how much of the burden the kind of advances funded address and the chance a year's portfolio delivers one (split below for reading). Worked out: coronary death rates in England and Wales fell 54% from 1981 to 2000, about 4% a year, and 42% of the fall came from treatments (Ünal, Critchley and Capewell, Circulation 2004, IMPACT), so treatment advances avert about 1.7% of a rich country's burden a year; high-income countries carry 19% of the world's cardiovascular DALYs (84 of 436 million, GBD 2023), so about 0.3% of the world burden, plus a lower rate in the rest of the world where uptake is low (a quarter of it on 81%: another 0.3%). Part of that is uptake of older advances rather than the year's new research: about half. So a year of the world's research averts about 0.3% of the burden, 0.05% to 1%.

rows.label: Share of that burden the advances from a year of the field's research avert once adopted
rows.explainer: For reading: the share of the burden the kind of advances funded (a new drug class, a device, a care pathway) address at the uptake they reach, a few percent each (SGLT2 inhibitors or PCSK9 inhibitors in their indications, primary angioplasty). The result reads only its product with p_success (share_burden_averted_per_research_year), so this split doesn't add a second range.

rows.label: Implied probability a year's portfolio of the field turns into such an advance in practice (for reading)
rows.explainer: The judged product over the judged share addressed: about 6%. For comparison, about 1 in 4 cardiovascular drugs entering phase 3 and well under 1 in 10 from phase 1 reach approval (Wong, Siah and Lo, Biostatistics 2019); BHF's portfolio is mostly basic and translational science.

rows.label: Years sooner the advance arrives because the field is funded this year
rows.explainer: Without a year of funding, the same advances would come later from the following years' research, industry and other countries; this is how much later. Its credit is split by BHF's share of the field's funding (research_attribution_share_shared), and it already answers "would it have happened anyway" (Convention 5), so there is no counterfactual adjustment as well. Anchored on the returns-to-research reference class: with the rest of the chain, 5 years makes a pound of BHF research about as productive in health as the 9% health-gain return of UK cardiovascular research implies in UK gains alone (ref_dalys_per_gbp against research_dalys_per_gbp_credited); 2 to 15 years.

rows.label: Years from the funding until the result is in practice

source.title: News-Medical, New report shows the financial and social value of investing in medical research (on HERG, OHE and RAND Europe, Medical Research: What's it worth?, 2008)
source.quote: a time lag between research expenditure and eventual health benefits of approximately 17 years.

rows.explainer: The lag the UK study of cardiovascular research found between research spending and health benefit; UK cancer research had about 15 years (Glover et al. 2014: an elapsed time of 15 years), and screening and guideline work is quicker (Morris, Wooding and Grant 2011). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the result is in practice
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years brought forward
Research: value of a cardiovascular death at 70 or older (world, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70–74 and 75–79 (their mean) and for 80 and over (80–84; 85 and over has the same weight), mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older.

rows.label: Research: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of cardiovascular deaths worldwide, two thirds of them at 70 or older (GBD 2023, facts: death_ages), 50–69 at the 50–74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights for 70–79 and 80 and over (references: families/high-income-care.md), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Research: deaths per DALY
rows.explainer: The burden is GBD DALYs, mostly years of life lost to deaths at GBD's life expectancy, which the value-of-a-life slider wouldn't touch. As everywhere on the site, each DALY is split into its illness part, kept as DALYs, and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age in units of value and brought into healthy years by the bridge (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4, and 2.6).

rows.label: Research: share of each DALY that is illness, not death
rows.explainer: Kept as healthy years; the rest of each DALY is deaths (the row above).

rows.label: Expected DALYs averted by the year's research of the whole field (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Healthy years averted by the year's research, in GBD's DALYs (deaths split out below).

rows.label: Reference class: health-gain return on UK cardiovascular research (internal rate of return)

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: This produced a best-estimate IRR of 10%, compared with 9% previously estimated for cardiovascular disease research.

rows.explainer: Context, for reading only (not on the result's path): For reading only (the sanity bound of references/families/medical-research.md): UK cardiovascular research's return in UK health gains, 9% a year; cancer's 10% is the high end.

rows.label: Reference class: lag from research spending to health gain
rows.explainer: The same 17-year lag as the chain.

rows.label: Reference class: the study's value of a QALY (£)

source.title: News-Medical, New report shows the financial and social value of investing in medical research (on Medical Research: What's it worth?, 2008)
source.quote: Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALY), estimated by NICE to be worth around £25,000 each.

rows.explainer: Context, for reading only (not on the result's path): The study's own conversion from health to money, used only to turn its return back into QALYs for the check; it moves nothing on the result's path.

rows.label: Reference class: UK healthy years per £ of research the return implies (for reading)
rows.explainer: A 9% return with a 17-year lag means each £ buys a stream of about £0.39 of UK health a year from year 17 on; at £25,000 a QALY and the shared discount rate that is about 0.0002 healthy years per £, in the UK alone, with UK research credited with 17% of UK gains (Glover et al.: "We related 17% of the annual NMB estimated to be attributable to UK research").

rows.label: The chain's healthy years per £ of BHF research, after its adjustments (for reading)
rows.explainer: In GBD's DALYs, before the deaths are valued by age, so in the reference's own units. Against ref_dalys_per_gbp: the chain gives about the same. The two count different things: the reference credits UK research with 17% of UK gains, far above the UK's few percent of the world's cardiovascular research funding, while the chain credits BHF its funding share of world gains. We take the agreement as the check and add no world spillover on top, since the 17% credit already counts UK research generously and uptake outside rich countries is low. In numbers: for the chain to match a UK-only reference while crediting BHF only its ~1% of world funding, world gains must be about ten times UK gains, plausible given the UK's small share of the world's cardiovascular burden and much lower uptake elsewhere. HERG's 9% is net of NHS treatment costs, so the reference is a lower bound on gross health gains.

rows.label: Advocacy: people aged 14 to 30 in England (2021)

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: The population of those aged 14 to 30 is 11,777,381

rows.explainer: The age group the impact assessment models the law's effect on smoking uptake in, from ONS 2021 mid-year estimates; with the number of single years of age it gives one year's cohort.

rows.label: Advocacy: single years of age from 14 to 30

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: The population of those aged 14 to 30 is 11,777,381

rows.explainer: Ages 14 to 30 inclusive are 17 single years, so the band divided by 17 is an average cohort.

rows.label: Advocacy: UK population ÷ England's

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: all the England estimates have been uplifted by 1.19 to provide estimates for the costs and benefits of the smokefree generation policy to the UK.

rows.explainer: The Act covers the whole UK; the impact assessment scales England by population, and so do we.

rows.label: Advocacy: people per year brought under the smokefree-generation law (one UK birth cohort)
rows.explainer: The Tobacco and Vapes Act (Royal Assent April 2026) bans the sale of tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. Each year the law is brought forward covers one more birth cohort, about 820,000 people in the UK; so the yearly flow the win counts is one cohort, and $win_years_counted counts the years.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of a covered cohort kept from smoking
rows.explainer: The impact assessment's central scenario (a 30% fall in the yearly rate of taking up smoking below the age of sale, picked with tobacco-control experts (19 consulted, 14 replied) and chosen over stronger scenarios to allow for underage sales and proxy purchases, paras 154-161) takes smoking among 14 to 30 year olds from 9.2% in the baseline to effectively zero, "9.2 percentage points lower in 2056" (para. 169). That is the high end. Our best guess, 8 points, takes a little off for a baseline already falling faster than the assessment's flat steady state (a criticism made to the Public Bill Committee); leakage is not taken off again here or in adv_evidence_adj. The low end, 2.5 points, is the assessment's weakest scenario (Scenario 5, 6.7% against 9.2%, Table 27). The figures are from the March 2024 impact assessment; the November 2024 one for the reintroduced bill keeps the same smokefree-generation modelling.

rows.label: Advocacy: lifetime DALYs lost per person who smokes as a young adult
rows.explainer: Doll et al.'s 50-year follow-up of British doctors (BMJ 2004): lifelong smokers die about 10 years sooner, and stopping at 30 avoids almost all of that, at 40 most of it. Many young smokers stop, so a person smoking at 14 to 30 loses a few healthy years on average, deaths and illness from heart disease, cancer and lung disease together. Check against the impact assessment: with the rest of the branch a covered UK cohort gains about 198,000 DALYs undiscounted (824,000 × 8% × 3), about 109,000 at the government's 1.5% over 40 years; the assessment's own figure, deaths only and only those before 2100, is about 950,000 QALYs in present value (£66.7bn at £70,000) over all the cohorts it covers, most of whose smoking deaths fall after 2100, so roughly nine cohorts' worth by our figure. Consistent within the range.

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the law biting on a cohort until its health gains
rows.explainer: Smoking kills and disables mostly in middle and old age: the impact assessment finds "no health benefits would be expected until 2044" (para. 178), 17 years after the law starts, with gains rising to 2100. A cohort kept from smoking at 18 has its gains mostly at 50 to 80, about 40 years later. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Advocacy: DALYs averted per person in a covered cohort (lifetime, discounted to the law's start)
rows.explainer: The share kept from smoking times the healthy years a young smoker loses, discounted over the decades until those years come. Per cohort member, so multiplied by one cohort per year counted.

rows.label: Policy: value of a smoking death at 70 or older (UK, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70–79 and for 80 and over, mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older.

rows.label: Policy: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of smoking deaths in the UK, two thirds of them at 70 or older (GBD 2023, facts: death_ages), 50–69 at the 50–74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights for 70–79 and 80 and over (references: families/high-income-care.md), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Policy: deaths per DALY
rows.explainer: The burden is GBD DALYs, mostly years of life lost to deaths at GBD's life expectancy, which the value-of-a-life slider wouldn't touch. As everywhere on the site, each DALY is split into its illness part, kept as DALYs, and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age in units of value and brought into healthy years by the bridge (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4, and 2.6).

rows.label: Policy: share of each DALY that is illness, not death
rows.explainer: Kept as healthy years; the rest of each DALY is deaths (the row above).

rows.label: Advocacy: share of all the campaigning behind the law done in this year
rows.explainer: The law is won (Royal Assent April 2026, three weeks after the year ends), so the question is how much of the win this year's work bought. The bill was introduced in November 2024 and spent this year in the House of Lords, the last stretch of a campaign that ran from the 2023 plan (and of decades of tobacco-control work before it); BHF's share of the people and money behind it is in adv_attribution_share_shared. A fifth, from about four years of active campaigning with the final year weighing more.

rows.label: Advocacy: years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the year modelled until the law takes effect
rows.explainer: The sale ban starts on 1 January 2027 (the impact assessment's appraisal starts on that date), about a year after the middle of the year modelled. The longer wait until the health gains is in adv_dalys_per_person_year.

rows.label: Advocacy: discounted years of impact
Expected DALYs averted by advocacy (before adjustments)
Implementation pilots: share of the UK cardiovascular burden in the group one pilot's model would serve nationally
rows.explainer: Each pilot serves a narrow group: women who had high blood pressure in pregnancy (about 10% of births, young and at low near-term risk), patients eligible for six-monthly cholesterol injections, taxi drivers, a screening population. Such a group carries of the order of a few hundredths to half a percent of the UK burden. Our judgment: 0.2%, 0.05% to 0.5%.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: share of the group's burden averted by the model of care at scale
rows.explainer: A delivery model reaches more people with a proven treatment, or reaches them sooner. A 5 mmHg fall in systolic blood pressure cuts major cardiovascular events by about 10% (Rahimi et al., Lancet 2021, 48 trials); a new service changes treatment for only part of its group, by part of that. Our judgment: 5% of the group's burden, 2% to 10%.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: share of the UK burden the year's pilots would avert if all were adopted
rows.explainer: The pilots in the year times the share of the burden in each one's group times the share of it the model averts: about 0.14% of the UK burden if every pilot were adopted everywhere.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: chance a pilot's model is adopted widely
rows.explainer: The chance a pilot's model is adopted widely. Reference class: of the NHS's five New Care Model (Vanguard) programmes, nationally funded to be spread, only one was scaled up (MacInnes et al., J Health Serv Res Policy 2023), and 'pilotitis', the repetition of pilots that never spread, is a recognised NHS problem (Scarbrough et al. 2023). Small grant-funded pilots spread less often than national programmes, though BHF renamed the fund to focus on adoption (p. 29). Our judgment: 15%, 5% to 30%.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: years a success is brought forward
rows.explainer: Without the pilot the same change of practice would come later, from NHS programmes, other funders' pilots or guidance catching up (the translation lag is shortest for care pathways: Morris, Wooding and Grant 2011). Our judgment: 3 years, 1 to 6.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: years from the award to health gains in wider use
rows.explainer: A pilot runs one to three years and is evaluated; adoption takes some years more, and lower blood pressure or cholesterol cuts events within a year or two. Our judgment: 5 years, 3 to 10.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: wait discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: discounted years brought forward
Implementation pilots: value of a cardiovascular death at 70 or older (UK, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70–79 and for 80 and over, mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of cardiovascular deaths in the UK, four in five at 70 or older (GBD 2023, facts: death_ages), 50–69 at the 50–74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights for 70–79 and 80 and over (references: families/high-income-care.md), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: deaths per DALY
rows.explainer: The burden is GBD DALYs, mostly years of life lost to deaths at GBD's life expectancy, which the value-of-a-life slider wouldn't touch. As everywhere on the site, each DALY is split into its illness part, kept as DALYs, and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age in units of value and brought into healthy years by the bridge (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4, and 2.6).

rows.label: Implementation pilots: share of each DALY that is illness, not death
rows.explainer: Kept as healthy years; the rest of each DALY is deaths (the row above).

rows.label: Implementation pilots: DALYs averted before adjustments
Research: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The research chain rests on judgments calibrated to returns-to-research studies, which their authors call best-case estimates (they credit research with health gains that also came from changes in behaviour and care, and take the best-documented diseases). 0.7, as the template's default for a chain anchored on aggregate studies rather than this charity's own results; the range runs to face value.

rows.label: Research: BHF's share of the world's cardiovascular research funding
rows.explainer: The years brought forward are the whole field's, so BHF is credited with its share of all funders' spending on it (about $127m of research a year). Anchors: BHF funded 52% (£85m) of UK public and charity cardiovascular research in 2022 (UKCRC, via BHF); the US NIH spends about $2.9bn a year on cardiovascular research and EU public and charity funders at least €1bn (CardioScape, 2010-2012), with Japan, China, Canada and Australia on top: about $5-6bn of non-commercial research. Industry is counted in full: private sources paid 58% of US medical research in 2012 (Moses et al., JAMA 2015, in resources), so all funders together spend about $13bn a year on cardiovascular research, of which BHF is about 1%. The range runs from industry at twice that share (0.5%) to the non-commercial funders alone (2%).

rows.label: Advocacy: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The effect of a generational sale ban is modelled, not observed (New Zealand repealed its own before it took effect); underage sales and leakage are already in the assessment's central scenario and adv_prevalence_cut, so this covers the rest: substitution by vaping (which the same Act regulates) and the chance of later repeal. 0.7, as the research branch.

rows.label: Advocacy: BHF's share of everyone's resources behind the law
rows.explainer: The government proposed and drafted the law, Parliament passed it, and many groups campaigned (Action on Smoking and Health, Cancer Research UK, the royal colleges, directors of public health, BHF). BHF part-funds ASH and campaigned itself; it says the law "would not have materialised without constant pressure from ASH, ourselves and other partners" (annual report p. 35). Government staff time counts among the resources (Convention 2). One in twenty, from BHF being one of the two largest health charities in a coalition of dozens behind a government bill.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: trust in the chain
rows.explainer: The chain is judgment anchored on trial effects of the treatments the pilots deliver (blood-pressure and cholesterol lowering), which delivery in the community may not reach, and pilots often report feasibility rather than outcomes. Our judgment: 0.6, 0.3 to 0.9, below research's 0.7 because the pilots are small and early.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: BHF's share of the resources behind the change
rows.explainer: As for research, credit is BHF's share of the resources behind the piloting and its evaluation, not of the cost of delivering a success later: BHF's award against the NHS trust's own staff time and facilities given to the pilot (Convention 2). For awards of £150,000 to £200,000 the award is most of it. Our judgment: BHF 60%, 40% to 80%.

rows.label: Research: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the chain is our judgment calibrated on returns-to-research studies; no measure of what BHF's own grants achieved exists. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Policy: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the law's health effect comes from the government's impact assessment (modelled, not observed) and BHF's part in it is our judgment. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Implementation pilots: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: this year's pilots have no results yet, so their value is our judgment anchored on trials of the treatments they deliver. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Research: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the years brought forward already say how much later the advance would have come without the year's funding (Convention 5).

rows.label: Policy: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: $win_years_counted already says how much later the law would have come without the campaign (Convention 5).

rows.label: Implementation pilots: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the years brought forward already say how much later the change of practice would have come without the pilot (Convention 5).

rows.label: Research: BHF's share of the credit
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the resources behind this branch's outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Policy: BHF's share of the credit
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the resources behind this branch's outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Implementation pilots: BHF's share of the credit
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the resources behind this branch's outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

Policy: product of adjustments
Implementation pilots: product of adjustments
Research: illness averted, credited (DALYs)
Research: deaths averted, credited and valued by age (units of value)
Policy: illness averted, credited (DALYs)

This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_attribution_share_shared + advocacy_dalys * adv_attribution_share_shared + impl_dalys * impl_attribution_share_shared) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + impl_dalys)
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the field's funding for research, of the campaign's resources for policy and of the resources behind a pilot's adoption: the DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_attribution_share + advocacy_dalys * adv_attribution_share + impl_dalys * impl_attribution_share) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + impl_dalys)
rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own share (research_, adv_, impl_attribution_share).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_evidence_adj + advocacy_dalys * adv_evidence_adj + impl_dalys * impl_evidence_adj) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + impl_dalys)
rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches' trust in their evidence, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Missing-data step (DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_missing_data_adj + advocacy_dalys * adv_missing_data_adj + impl_dalys * impl_missing_data_adj) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + impl_dalys)
rows.explainer: Every branch is thin, so each reads the shared slider; this average is for reading only.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_counterfactual_adj + advocacy_dalys * adv_counterfactual_adj + impl_dalys * impl_counterfactual_adj) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + impl_dalys)
rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: 1 in every branch (research_, adv_, impl_counterfactual_adj), since the years brought forward and the years a won law counts already say what would have happened anyway (Convention 5).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_total_adj + advocacy_dalys * adv_total_adj + impl_dalys * impl_total_adj) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + impl_dalys)
rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches' products of adjustments (research_, adv_, impl_total_adj), for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Benefits not counted: the Act's limits on youth vaping, second-hand smoke averted (both left out by the impact assessment's health figures), the research workforce and infrastructure BHF trains and builds that later research uses. Harms: research effort drawn from other diseases (BHF's leverage of other funders' money is not counted as a gain either). Also BHF's other policy work, whose cost is in policy_share_of_health: the Modern Service Framework for cardiovascular disease in England's 10-year plan, the Scottish Government's £2.5m for cardiac arrest survival (February 2026) and the extended blood-pressure framework in Wales (p. 34-35), about 2% of the result if worth about half the tobacco branch. Positive on balance: 8%, -5% to 25%.

rows.label: Value in units of value (none: the burden is counted in DALYs), in GiveWell units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The deaths inside every branch's DALYs, valued by age in units of value with each branch's own adjustments; the bridge below brings them into healthy years by the shared conversion.

rows.label: Value in units of value (none: the burden is counted in DALYs), in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Life satisfaction (none measured), in wellbeing-adjusted life years (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: neither branch has evidence in life-satisfaction terms; their good is counted as healthy years.

rows.label: Life satisfaction (none measured), in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Healthy years counted directly (before adjustments)
rows.formula: research_dalys * research_yld_share + advocacy_dalys * adv_yld_share + impl_dalys * impl_yld_share
rows.explainer: The illness part of each branch's DALYs, before adjustments (the deaths go through uov_bridged).

rows.label: Years of healthy life
rows.formula: (research_illness_credited + adv_illness_credited + impl_illness_credited + dalys_from_uov + dalys_from_wellby * total_adj) * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch's illness with its own adjustments, plus the deaths through the bridge (already adjusted branch by branch, Convention 4), times the unmodelled share.

BHF's own staff pay as a share of research cost

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, note 4 gross expenditure

rows.explainer: BHF's own staff over the full cost modelled (Convention 1). Research: £1.9m of staff and £1.7m of allocated support costs (almost all staff) of £96.2m; the policy and pilot share (11%) of health's £6.4m staff and £6.1m support; and fundraising staff, £19.8m of the £46.2m of fundraising costs (note 4, p. 125), spread over all charitable spending like the overhead (13p a pound of programme). About £5.0m on £102.2m plus 13% of it, over 1.38 times the programme cost: 13%, 10% to 16%. The researchers the grants pay are university staff, whose pay is the grants' cost, not BHF staff's forgone salary.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: BHF's staff are UK charity staff (grant managers, policy and support staff): the shared gap for UK charities.
